title: Three words for soul
hook: nefesh, ruach and neshamah, all tied to breath and wind

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ch-Y-H, the root of chai and chayim, and a law read as live by them, not die by them. Your line was l'chaim. Did you lift a cup to something alive? Today, what the Torah says makes a body alive at all. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-three.

Before the coffee, before the phone, there's a short prayer in the morning service that speaks about the soul. Its opening runs something like this: my God, the soul you placed in me is pure. You created it, you formed it, you breathed it into me, and you keep it inside me. Read it slowly and one verb jumps out. Breathed. Not built, not installed. Breathed. The prayer is leaning on a scene from the start of Genesis, where God bends over a figure of earth and breathes. And it turns out Hebrew doesn't have just one word for what English calls a soul. It has several. Today, three of them, and one verse where a breath passes between two.
screen: `A MORNING PRAYER.` → `YOU BREATHED IT INTO ME.` → `MORE THAN ONE WORD FOR SOUL.`

segments.voice: Three words. Take them one at a time, then together. First, nefesh. In the creation story the animals are called nefesh chayah, living creatures, and so, a chapter later, is the first human. Nefesh is the whole living being: the self that gets hungry, tired and scared. Second, ruach. In the second verse of Genesis, the King James says "the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters." The Hebrew under Spirit is ruach. After the flood, when "God made a wind to pass over the earth," that wind is ruach too. Same word: translators reach for spirit in one place and wind in another, and the Hebrew holds both at once. Third, neshamah, breath, the word the morning prayer uses. Now put them together, in Genesis chapter two, in the King James: "and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Breath of life: nishmat chayim, the neshamah. Living soul: nefesh chayah. Two of the three words share one sentence, and the thing between them is a breath. Later teachers, in the midrash and among the mystics, read these words as different sides or layers of the soul. Some readers keep it plainer. In this verse, a soul begins as something breathed in. You can't see it, but you can hear it, and you're doing it right now.
screen: `NEFESH: A WHOLE LIVING BEING.` · `RUACH: WIND, BREATH, SPIRIT.` · `NESHAMAH: THE BREATH OF LIFE.` · `ONE VERSE HOLDS TWO OF THEM.` · then, large: `נֶפֶשׁ · רוּחַ · נְשָׁמָה`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: three deep breaths, then quiet. Settle, and let your shoulders drop. Breathe in through your nose, slowly, all the way down, and let it out. That's one. Breathe in again and notice the air arriving, cool at the nostrils, the same place the verse puts it. Let it out. That's two. One more, and on the way out, let the word neshamah ride the breath, silently. Then stop counting and just let the breath come on its own. If you pray, you can say the morning prayer's thought in your own way: the soul you placed in me is pure. The bell holds the time.
Three words for soul. Nefesh, a living being. Ruach, wind and spirit. Neshamah, breath. Today's word.

Your line: soul is breath. Today, the next time you're rushed or tense, take one slow breath through your nose before you answer, and notice it coming in. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: In the morning service Jews say Elohai neshamah, a blessing that thanks God for the pure soul placed within; teachers in the midrash and in Jewish mysticism speak of nefesh, ruach and neshamah as layers of the soul.

myth: Hebrew has exactly one word for soul
it has several, and nefesh, ruach and neshamah all sit close to breath and wind.
in Genesis the animals are called nefesh chayah too
living creatures: the same words used for the first human a chapter later.
the morning prayer says the soul was built inside a person
it says God breathed it in.

fork.setup: you're translating Genesis 8:1, after the flood. the Hebrew says God sent a ruach over the earth. which English word do you choose?
fork.reveal: the King James chose wind: "God made a wind to pass over the earth." in Genesis 1:2 the same word became Spirit.

original.note: Hebrew: breath, and soul, as in nishmat chayim, the breath of life.

trapdoor: what you thought: a soul is one invisible thing with one name.
what it means: Hebrew uses nefesh, ruach and neshamah, a living being, a wind, a breath.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 2:7 puts two of them in one sentence: nishmat chayim, the breath of life, and nefesh chayah, a living soul.

notes: Genesis quotations taken from the KJV, which is on the public-domain list; JPS 1917 wording is close. Confirm the Judaism path is content with KJV here.
Elohai neshamah paraphrased ('the soul you placed in me is pure... you breathed it into me... you keep it inside me'); source Berakhot 60b and the siddur. Confirm the paraphrase is fair.
Genesis 1:24 and 2:7 both use nefesh chayah; confirm. Genesis 1:2 and 8:1 both use ruach; confirm.
Genesis Rabbah 14:9 lists names of the soul; the script says only that later teachers built these words into layers, without a count.
The index hook says 'all tied to breath and wind'; the script ties ruach and neshamah to breath and wind by the texts and calls nefesh a living being, which is the safer claim.
